title: How Leaders Treat Failure and Error Differently
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article draws a deliberate distinction between failure and error, arguing good leaders treat them as fundamentally different categories requiring different responses. Failure is framed as a collective, systemic event best examined in a group setting focused on future action rather than blame; error is framed as an individual misstep best corrected through a private conversation to avoid embarrassment and defensiveness. The piece also flags a language habit worth correcting — labeling a person 'a failure' creates lasting stigma, whereas framing outcomes as correctable errors preserves confidence. The closing metaphor casts failure as a group detour and errors as fillable potholes.
points: Failure is treated as a group event with shared contribution and discussed collectively, while errors are treated as individual missteps best addressed privately.
Group discussion of failure reduces defensiveness by shifting focus from blame to process improvement and future action.
Private discussion of individual errors allows correction without the embarrassment that group settings would create, making people more receptive.
Leaders discourage team members from labeling themselves or others as 'a failure,' since that permanent framing damages confidence and blocks learning, unlike correctable errors.
quotes: For leaders, failure is an event and a group activity. In other words, no one person fails. Failure is an outcome that many people contribute to.
Discussing failure in a group makes everyone accountable. Good leaders search less for reasons why something failed and spend more time on what to do differently in the future.
In contrast to failure, errors are mistakes, missteps, or oversights made by an individual. That makes discussing an error more effective if done privately, between the leader and the offender.
The permanent casting of failure when applied to individuals is a stigma that prevents people from learning and lowers confidence.
If failure is a group detour, errors are potholes that can be filled in. Neither is the opposite of success. Both pave the road for good fortune if addressed correctly.
